title: Bonds
intro: A bond is a loan you make to a government or company in exchange for regular interest and your money back at the end. Bonds are the anchor of most portfolios: steadier than stocks, a source of income, and often a cushion when stocks fall. Their prices still move, and the reason they move is the most important idea in fixed income: bond prices and interest rates go in opposite directions.

blocks.text: The parts of a bond

items: Face value (par, principal): the amount repaid at maturity, usually \$1,000 for a US bond (prices are quoted per 100 of face).
Coupon: the yearly interest as a percentage of face, paid usually twice a year in the US and UK, once a year for euro bonds. A 4% coupon on \$1,000 pays \$40 a year, as two \$20 payments.
Maturity: the date the principal is repaid. Short-term is under about 3 years, intermediate 3 to 10, long-term beyond.
Issuer: a government, government agency, city or state, or company. Who owes you the money decides the credit risk.
Zero-coupon bond: pays no coupon and is sold below face; your return is the climb to par. US Treasury bills are zeros, and Treasury STRIPS split coupon bonds into zeros.
Callable bond: the issuer may repay early, which it will do when rates fall, just when you'd least want your money back. You are paid a higher yield for that risk.

blocks.text: Price and yield

A bond's price is the present value of its cash flows at the market's current required rate, its yield to maturity (YTM). For a bond with coupon $C$ per period, face $F$ and $n$ periods left, at yield $y$ per period:

The YTM is the single rate that makes this sum equal the price: the bond's internal rate of return if you hold to maturity and reinvest the coupons at the same yield. When market yields rise, the fixed coupons are worth less, so the price falls. Three cases:

items: Coupon rate = yield: the bond trades at par (100).
Coupon rate < yield: it trades at a discount, below 100, and the climb to par makes up the shortfall.
Coupon rate > yield: it trades at a premium, above 100.

blocks.text: The current yield is coupon / price, the cash yield today; it ignores the gain or loss to par, so YTM is the better measure. For a callable bond also look at yield to call and yield to worst, the lowest yield across all the dates the issuer could repay.
Clean and dirty prices

Between coupon dates the seller has earned part of the next coupon. The buyer pays the quoted clean price plus accrued interest; the total is the dirty or full price. Quoting clean prices keeps the price from jumping on every coupon date.
Duration: how much a bond moves
Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time until you get your cash back:
For a zero-coupon bond it equals the maturity; coupons pull it shorter. Modified duration $D = D_{Mac}/(1 + y)$ (per period's compounding) gives the price sensitivity directly:

A bond fund with duration 6 loses about 6% if yields rise one percentage point, and gains about 6% if they fall one point. This is the single most useful number about a bond or bond fund. Duration is longer for longer maturities, lower coupons and lower yields. In 2022, when US yields rose about 2.5 points, long Treasury funds with duration near 17 lost around 30%: duration told you in advance roughly how much they could.
Dollar duration or DV01 (the dollar value of a 0.01% move, one basis point) is the same idea in money: $DV01 \approx D \times P \times 0.0001$.
Convexity
The price-yield curve is not a straight line; it bends upward. Duration is its slope, convexity $C$ its curvature, and adding it improves the estimate for larger moves:

Positive convexity means the bond gains more when yields fall than it loses when they rise by the same amount: good for the holder. Callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities have negative convexity at low yields: when rates fall the borrower refinances, so the price gains are capped.
Try a 30-year zero (coupon 0, maturity 30): its price swings wildly with yield. Then a 2-year bond: it barely moves. That is why money you need soon belongs in short bonds.
The risks of owning bonds

items: Interest rate risk: prices fall when yields rise. Measured by duration.

Reinvestment risk: if rates fall, coupons and maturing bonds must be reinvested at lower yields. Short bonds have much of this, long bonds little. At a holding period about equal to its duration, price risk and reinvestment risk roughly offset, which is the idea behind immunization.
Credit (default) risk: the issuer might not pay. Measured by ratings and the credit spread, the extra yield over a government bond of the same maturity.
Inflation risk: a fixed coupon buys less if inflation rises. Inflation-linked bonds address it.
Liquidity risk: many bonds trade rarely; selling quickly can mean a poor price.
Call and prepayment risk: your high-coupon bond is repaid early when rates fall.
Currency risk: a bond in another currency adds that currency's swings, often larger than the bond's own.

blocks.text: Individual bonds or bond funds

An individual bond held to maturity gives a known nominal return (if the issuer pays), and its price swings along the way don't matter if you never sell. A bond fund never matures: it keeps rolling into new bonds, so it has a roughly constant duration and no fixed end value. The economics are closer than they look, since both lose market value when rates rise and both then earn the higher yields. Funds give diversification and liquidity at a small cost; individual Treasuries or CDs give certainty for a specific future bill. A bond ladder (bonds maturing each year for several years) is a common middle path.
What bonds do in a portfolio

High-quality government bonds have often risen when stocks fell sharply (2008, early 2020), because investors flee to safety and central banks cut rates. That makes them a diversifier, not just a lower-return asset. The relationship is not guaranteed: when inflation is the problem, as in the 1970s and 2022, stocks and bonds can fall together.
Practice

blocks.title: Pricing a bond
blocks.text: A 3-year bond has a 5% annual coupon (paid yearly) and face 100. What is its price at a yield of 6%?
solution: It trades below par because its coupon is below the market yield.

blocks.title: Duration in use
blocks.text: A bond fund has a modified duration of 6.5 and yields 4.5%. If yields rise 0.8 points tomorrow, roughly what does the fund lose? About how long until the higher yield makes it back?
solution: The fund now yields about 5.3%, 0.8 points more than before; at that extra income it takes roughly $5.2/0.8 \approx 6.5$ years, about one duration, to catch up with where it would have been.

blocks.title: Zero-coupon bond
blocks.text: A 10-year zero-coupon bond yields 4% (annual compounding). What is its price per 100 face, and its Macaulay and modified duration?
solution: Macaulay duration = 10 years (the only cash flow is at year 10); modified $= 10/1.04 \approx 9.62$.

blocks.title: Convexity matters for big moves
blocks.text: A long bond has modified duration 17 and convexity 400. Estimate its price change for a 2-point rise in yields, with and without convexity.
solution: With convexity: $-34\% + \tfrac12 \times 400 \times 0.02^2 = -34\% + 8\% = -26\%$. For big moves the duration line overstates losses (and understates gains).
